promptText: Does streaming a model's response reduce the total time the model takes to generate that response (TTLT)?
options: Yes, streaming makes the model generate tokens faster
No -- TTLT is unchanged; streaming only changes when the user is allowed to see output that is already being produced (TTFT)
Yes, but only for responses longer than 500 tokens
No, streaming actually increases total generation time due to per-chunk overhead
explanation: Streaming does not change total generation time at all; it changes the user's experience of that time by delivering content at TTFT instead of making them wait silently until TTLT.

promptText: What does .stream() return from Spring AI's ChatClient, compared to .call()?
options: .call() returns Flux<ChatResponse>; .stream() returns a single ChatResponse
.stream() returns Flux<ChatResponse> (or Flux<String> via .content()), a cold reactive sequence of incremental chunks; .call() returns one complete response after blocking
Both return identical types; the only difference is internal buffering
.stream() requires a WebSocket connection while .call() does not
explanation: .call() blocks until generation finishes and returns one complete ChatResponse, while .stream() returns a cold Flux of incremental response chunks that begins producing values only once subscribed to.

promptText: Which transport do most LLM providers and Spring AI-based chat features use for streaming responses, and why?
options: WebSockets, because bidirectional push is required for token generation
Server-Sent Events (SSE), because the interaction is one-directional (server pushes tokens) and SSE survives ordinary HTTP infrastructure more easily
Raw TCP sockets, bypassing HTTP entirely
FTP, because it supports incremental file transfer
explanation: SSE is the simpler, one-directional half of what WebSockets offer, and because it rides on plain HTTP it survives ordinary proxies and load balancers far more easily than a WebSocket upgrade.

promptText: Why does calling .block() anywhere inside a Spring AI streaming pipeline defeat the purpose of streaming?
options: .block() is not a valid method on a Flux and will fail to compile
It forces the reactive chain to wait for the entire Flux to complete before returning anything, reintroducing full buffering identical in effect to never streaming
.block() only affects error handling, not the actual chunk delivery timing
.block() converts the response into a WebSocket connection automatically
explanation: .block() waits for the whole Flux to complete before returning a value, which reintroduces full server-side buffering and, on a WebFlux event-loop thread, also stalls that thread for other concurrent requests.

promptText: In reactive programming terms, is an LLM streaming call exposed via ChatModel.stream(...) a hot or cold publisher?
options: Hot -- tokens start generating the moment the Flux object is created, regardless of subscription
Cold -- nothing is sent to the provider and no tokens are generated until something subscribes to the returned Flux
It depends on which model provider is used
Neither concept applies to Flux<ChatResponse>
explanation: Building the Flux pipeline (attaching advisors, mapping, filtering) costs nothing and starts nothing; only the terminal subscription actually triggers the network call and starts burning tokens.

promptText: A streaming chat feature works perfectly on localhost but appears to deliver the entire response all at once once deployed behind NGINX. What is the most likely cause?
options: NGINX doesn't support HTTP at all
NGINX buffers proxied responses by default, accumulating the entire response before forwarding it downstream
Spring Boot automatically disables streaming when deployed to a non-local environment
The model provider throttles streaming requests from unrecognized IP ranges
explanation: NGINX buffers proxied HTTP responses by default; the fix is disabling buffering for that route (e.g., proxy_buffering off; or the X-Accel-Buffering: no response header).

promptText: What does backpressure actually protect against in the specific case of LLM token streaming, given that a hosted model generates tokens at its own pace regardless of the consumer?
options: It prevents the model provider from generating tokens too quickly for the network to handle

It protects a slow consumer inside your own application (e.g., a slow WebSocket client or downstream sink) from being handed data faster than it can process, which would otherwise grow an unbounded buffer
It throttles the model's inference speed directly via an API parameter
It has no practical effect for LLM streaming and exists only for database streams
explanation: You cannot signal a hosted provider to generate slower; what backpressure protects is your own application's consumer from being overwhelmed by data faster than it can process it.

promptText: Why can't a mid-stream provider error (e.g., a rate limit hit partway through generation) be reported to the client as an HTTP 500 status code?
options: HTTP 500 is reserved exclusively for database errors, not model errors
The 200 OK status and headers were already sent the instant streaming began, so an in-band error signal inside the stream itself is required instead
Spring WebFlux does not support non-200 status codes for any response type
SSE connections cannot carry error information under any circumstances
explanation: Because headers including the status code are committed the moment the first chunk is sent, a later failure must be encoded as a special event or payload inside the stream itself, not a changed HTTP status.

promptText: Why must an Advisor that persists conversation memory be adapted when the underlying call switches from .call() to .stream()?
options: Memory advisors are incompatible with streaming and must be disabled entirely
It must aggregate the arriving chunks into the full assistant message before writing to the memory store, without buffering the client-facing stream itself
Streaming responses cannot be written to a ChatMemoryRepository under any implementation
The advisor must switch from Java to a different reactive library entirely
explanation: A memory-persisting advisor must reconstruct the complete assistant text from all deltas before saving it, typically via a side-channel tap on the Flux, while still forwarding each chunk unbuffered to the caller.

promptText: According to Little's Law (L = lambda x W), if a service receives 40 new streaming chat requests per second and each stream takes an average of 5 seconds end to end, roughly how many concurrent open streaming connections should it expect at steady state, and why does this matter for capacity planning?
options: 8 connections; streaming connections are shorter-lived than normal requests

200 connections; because a streaming response holds a connection open for its full generation duration, a thread-per-request Servlet stack would need 200 threads pinned simultaneously, favoring a reactive stack instead
45 connections; Little's Law only applies to database connection pools
5 connections; concurrency equals the average stream duration alone
explanation: L = lambda x W = 40 x 5 = 200 concurrent connections at steady state, which on a thread-per-request stack means 200 threads pinned for the full duration -- exactly the capacity wall a reactive stack avoids.

promptText: Why does a delta emitted from a streaming LLM response not necessarily align with a single token, word, or JSON structural boundary?
options: Spring AI guarantees word-aligned chunking by default, so this is a non-issue

Providers stream text increments whose granularity can be a sub-word fragment, a single token, or a small batch of tokens depending on internal buffering -- only the full concatenation is guaranteed to reconstruct the exact response
Deltas are always exactly one UTF-8 character each
Chunk boundaries are configurable per request and always match sentence boundaries
explanation: What Spring AI guarantees is that concatenating every delta's text in arrival order reconstructs the full response exactly; delta granularity itself is an implementation detail you should not build fragile assumptions on.

promptText: When a model streams a tool/function call whose arguments arrive as JSON split across multiple chunks, what must the consuming application do?
options: Parse each chunk independently as its own complete JSON object
Buffer and reassemble the full arguments across chunks before attempting to parse the JSON, since a half-arrived JSON fragment will simply fail to parse
Discard tool-call chunks entirely since streaming doesn't support tool calling
Convert each chunk to XML before parsing, since JSON cannot be streamed
explanation: Tool-call arguments often arrive as a streamed, partial JSON fragment across chunks; the application must buffer and reassemble the complete arguments before parsing or executing the call.

promptText: A system streams raw model output directly to the user while a content-safety check runs in parallel. What architectural trade-off does this create, and what's a common mitigation?
options: There is no real trade-off; parallel safety checks are strictly better in every dimension

A user could see and screenshot content that a completeness check would have blocked before the block takes effect; a common mitigation is buffering a small look-ahead window or running lightweight per-chunk streaming-safe classifiers instead of naive stream-then-moderate-after
Parallel safety checks always run faster than the model itself, so timing is never an issue
The mitigation is to disable streaming entirely for any application with safety requirements
explanation: Streaming raw output while moderation runs afterward exposes content a completeness check would have blocked; systems with strict requirements buffer a look-ahead window or use per-chunk streaming-safe classifiers instead.

promptText: Why does applying a non-streaming-aware safety filter to a stream by buffering the entire response first architecturally undermine the point of streaming, even though the code technically still 'uses' Flux?
options: It doesn't undermine anything -- buffering before filtering has zero effect on user-perceived latency
It reintroduces the full TTLT wait the feature was meant to eliminate, since nothing reaches the user until the complete text is available for the filter to evaluate
Flux-based buffering is always faster than a raw blocking call, so this is actually an optimization
It only affects error handling, not the timing of chunk delivery to the client
explanation: If a moderation layer must see the complete text before releasing anything, the architecture has reintroduced the TTLT wait the whole streaming feature was meant to eliminate -- a deliberate trade-off, not an accident.

promptText: Why does a blocking call (e.g., a synchronous JDBC lookup) inside a custom streaming Advisor pose a qualitatively different risk on a WebFlux stack than the same blocking call would on a traditional thread-per-request Servlet stack?
options: WebFlux does not permit blocking calls to compile at all, so this scenario cannot occur

On WebFlux, a small fixed number of event-loop threads serve many concurrent streams, so one blocked thread can stall every other concurrent stream sharing it -- a failure mode that doesn't exist when each request already has its own dedicated thread
Blocking calls are only dangerous on the Servlet stack, never on WebFlux
The risk is identical on both stacks since Java threads behave the same way regardless of framework
explanation: A reactive stack trades lower per-connection resource cost for the requirement that nothing blocks the event loop; one blocking call can stall an event-loop thread and degrade every other concurrent stream sharing it.
